bt67yj-k39009-d1e106.summary: This paragraph is the rubric heading announcing distinction 37 and its first section, stating the topic to be treated: that God is everywhere and in all things, and this in three ways.

bt67yj-k39009-d1e117.summary: The paragraph argues, on the authority of Scripture (Jeremiah 23, Wisdom 1, Psalm 138, Job 11) and the Fathers (Gregory, Augustine, the Glossa ordinaria), that God is truly and properly in all things, and in all places insofar as places are themselves things, and it introduces the traditional threefold distinction of the modes by which God is said to be in creatures: by power, by presence, and by essence.
claims: God is truly and conformably said by Scripture to be in all things.
Since God fills all things, and whatever is in all things is also in all places, God is everywhere according to the Catholic faith.
There are three ways in which God is understood to be in all created things: through power, presence, and essence.
God's presence in things by these three modes commends divine providence against those who deny God's immediate governance of creatures.

bt67yj-k39009-d1e230.summary: The paragraph explains the mode of divine presence 'by presence' (per praesentiam): God sees and beholds all things that happen anywhere, as if laid open before his sight, in the way a person is said to be present to what he looks upon. This mode commends God's providence and knowledge of individual things, against those who deny that God attends to particulars.
claims: God is said to be in all things by presence because all things that happen anywhere are seen and beheld by him as if placed in his sight.
This mode of presence commends divine providence and knowledge of singular things, against those who deny that God attends to the particulars of the world.

bt67yj-k39009-d1e281.summary: The paragraph explains the mode of divine presence 'by essence' (per essentiam) according to some authors: God's nature or substance is nowhere absent and is wholly present in itself to each and every thing, a mode proper to God alone though faintly imaged in how the soul is wholly present in the whole body and in each of its parts.
claims: According to some, God is said to be in all things by essence because his substance is nowhere absent and is wholly and intimately present, in itself, to every single thing.
This mode is proper to God alone and incommunicable, though the soul's presence to the whole body and its parts offers a faint vestige or image of it.
concepts: incommunicability of the divine mode of presence

bt67yj-k39009-d1e321.summary: The paragraph reports that Aquinas explains the mode 'by essence' somewhat differently: God's essence, being absolute and separate from every creature, is in a creature only insofar as it is applied to it through operation; hence God is in things by presence (as the operator must be present to what is operated on), by power (since the operation does not depart from the divine power from which it proceeds), and by essence (since that power is identical with the divine essence). The paragraph then reports the Master's (Peter Lombard's) objection that this explanation is insufficient, since 'God is everywhere by essence' contains more than a living person can grasp, and notes that Aquinas himself, in expounding the text, concedes that those who explained the mode this way did not sufficiently explain it, and instead clarifies (in the Summa) that God is in all things by essence insofar as he is present to all as the cause of their being.
claims: Aquinas explains that God is in a thing by presence, by power, and by essence in a single interconnected way rooted in operation and the identity of divine power with divine essence.
The Master (Lombard) objects that this explanation, though true, does not capture the full sense of 'God is everywhere by essence.'

Aquinas himself later concedes the insufficiency of that earlier explanation and clarifies, in the Summa, that God is in things by essence inasmuch as his substance is present to all as the cause of being.
concepts: identity of divine power and essence
reception and correction of a theological explanation across works

bt67yj-k39009-d1e411.summary: The paragraph raises and resolves an objection: how does the mode 'by essence' differ from the mode 'by power,' since by power too God is in all things as cause of being? Following Cajetan, it distinguishes immediacy of power (respecting all things universally, as to everything about them) from immediacy of essence/suppositum (respecting all things, but only as to their very act of being). It further notes that those the Master reprehends acknowledged God's immediate presence by power but not by essence, which is contrary to Catholic truth, citing Acts 17 ('in him we live and move and have our being').
claims: The mode by power and the mode by essence differ: power implies immediacy of virtue with respect to everything about all things, whereas essence implies immediacy of the divine suppositum with respect only to the very being of each thing.
Denying God's immediate presence by essence, while granting it by power, is contrary to Catholic truth.
concepts: immediacy of virtue vs. immediacy of suppositum
power (potentia) vs. essence (essentia) as modes of presence

bt67yj-k39009-d1e459.summary: A brief closing paragraph directing the reader to further discussion of God's existing-in-all-things in Augustine's Letter 57 to Dardanus and in Book 8 of On Genesis Against the Manichees, chapter 26.

bt67yj-k39009.summary: Capitulum 1 of Estius's commentary on distinction 37 establishes, against Scripture and the Fathers, that God is everywhere and in all things, and expounds the classic threefold scholastic distinction of the modes of divine presence — by power, by presence, and by essence — surveying both the standard account and Aquinas's own refinement of the mode 'by essence,' and resolving the apparent overlap between the modes of power and essence via Cajetan's distinction between immediacy of virtue and immediacy of suppositum.
claims: God is truly present in all things and all places, per Scripture and patristic authority.
There are three distinct modes of divine presence in creatures: by power, by presence, and by essence.

The mode 'by essence' admits of more than one theological account, and later authors (including Aquinas himself) refined the earlier explanation to say God is present by essence insofar as he is the cause of being to all things.

The modes of power and essence are formally distinct: power concerns immediacy of virtue over everything about a thing; essence concerns immediacy of the divine suppositum with respect to the thing's very being.
